newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Vegetable oil markets take Deng's death in stride.
newsitem.headline: Vegetable oil markets take Deng's death in stride.

text.p: Southeast Asian vegetable oil markets conducted business as usual on Thursday, underpinned by confidence that market reforms initated by China's Deng Xiaoping had taken root and could not be reversed following his death.

Regional traders said the Malaysian palm oil market was more concerned over an Indian government proposal to raise the import duty on edible oils, while their Indonesian counterparts ganged up to raise domestic palm olein, or cooking oil, prices.
Filipino traders were resigned to the fact the Chinese could live without their coconut oil, but were expecting higher prices due to rains in a key growing region.
"Deng's death had no impact at all," one Singapore trader who does business with China told Reuters.

"He has been ill for a long time, and his death was not totally unexpected," he said. "I don't expect his passing to have any impact on China's buying programme, because players there are now more professional and market orientated."
China on Thursday began six days of mourning for paramount leader Deng who transformed the world's most populous nation from backward Stalinist state to economic powerhouse.
The gravel-voiced veteran of military battlefields and backroom political struggles died at 9.08 p.m. (1308 GMT) on Wednesday in Beijing, the official Xinhua news agency said.
His pragmatic market reforms propelled China onto the world stage as an emerging economic superpower.

China bought 1.05 million tonnes of crude palm oil products in 1995 such as palm stearin and refined bleached and deodorised palm oil for the making of items such as margarine and soap, but its purchases fell to 873,118 tonnes in 1996.
The country's purchase order depends largely on prices and to a certain extent on weather, switching palm oil products with soyoil, which is more suitable during winter months.
"There seems to be less red tape in doing business with China these days," one trader said. "Payments are no longer problems, despite the occasional default or delay."
"China either buys directly or through its companies in Hong Kong," the Indonesian trader said. "But most of its purchases are from Malaysia where the products market is more active."
He said barring any major political upheavel in the succession process in China, he did not expect Deng's death to have any impact on the Indonesian market.

"Why should his death affect the market? It should not affect China's buying programme either," said a Malaysian trader. "The market is down this morning but this has nothing to do with Deng's death. There are other factors."
A Filipino trader said China depended largely on soyoil, and could well do without coconut oil from the Philippines.
"China imports largely soya. They can live without coconut oil," the trader said.
Traders said coconut oil prices were expect to rise due to rains on Mindanao island, which accounts for 55 percent of Philippine coconut ouput and 80 percent of the country's coconut oil exports.
"Coconut oil is now trading at $800 per tonne in Manila as against $725 per tonne FOB of the commodity for nearby months in Europe," one trader said.
